summary: Discusses the error-detection codes used by iSCSI and the considerations behind choosing a CRC or checksum for it. It looks at how well cyclic redundancy checks detect undetected errors and what that means for storage traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: When data travels over a wire it can get flipped by accident. This document explains how a special number added to each message helps spot the damage, and why a certain kind was chosen.

questions: why is crc better than checksums
subtitle: Analyzing error detection codes for reliable storage over IP networks

tldr.problem: iSCSI sends storage traffic (block data) over IP networks where bits can be corrupted by noise, memory errors, or software bugs. Choosing the right error detection code means keeping the probability of undetected errors extremely low while managing hardware complexity.
tldr.mechanism: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) polynomials detect the vast majority of errors by calculating parity bits that reveal when received data differs from transmitted data. CRC32C is superior to alternatives like checksums because it detects burst errors and independent bit errors with near-zero false negatives.
tldr.outcome: CRC32C is recommended for iSCSI, offering undetected error probabilities around 10^-40 for 8 kilobyte blocks and handling petabytes of data without missing corruptions.

today: RFC 3385 remains the authoritative analysis of error detection for iSCSI. CRC32C, as recommended by this RFC, is used in the iSCSI specification (RFC 7143) for protecting header and data digests. The analysis here continues to inform choices about error detection in storage and other reliability-critical protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC analyzes Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) codes and other error-detection mechanisms to help choose an appropriate error detection code for iSCSI (Internet Protocol Small Computer System Interface), which carries block storage traffic over IP networks.

CRC codes have been adopted in communications and storage standards (ATM, IEEE, CCITT, and others) because they offer very low probabilities of undetected errors, are simple to implement in hardware, and are effective at detecting both burst errors (consecutive bit errors) and scattered independent bit errors. The probability of undetected errors depends on the polynomial chosen to generate the code, the error distribution (error model), and the data length.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains how to pick a mathematical formula that spots when data gets damaged during transmission. CRCs are fast, simple, and very good at catching corruption.

sections.title: Error Models and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes error detection code behavior under two conditions: noisy channels with burst errors (consecutive corrupted bits) and low-noise channels with independent single bit errors. Burst errors are more common in practice due to physical phenomena like temporary line noise or memory errors affecting multiple adjacent bits.

For iSCSI, the RFC targets extremely low undetected error probabilities. Because iSCSI systems must reliably transport petabytes of data (10^16 bits) without undetected errors, the document uses reference probabilities of 10^-23 and 10^-45—physical limits inspired by Avogadro's number and the number of atoms in the known universe. For 8 kilobyte blocks (64 kilobits), this translates to per-bit undetected error probabilities between 10^-28 and 10^-50.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets extremely strict goals: errors should be so rare that they almost never happen, even if you send massive amounts of data for years.

sections.title: CRC Theory and Polynomials
sections.content:
A CRC code consists of information bits plus parity bits computed from those information bits using a generator polynomial. The core principle is that undetected errors occur only when the error pattern itself is a valid codeword—an extremely rare occurrence if the polynomial is chosen correctly.

The performance of a CRC code is measured by analyzing its weight distribution: the count of codewords having each weight (number of 1-bits). Historical research by mathematicians like Wolf and Castagnoli has shown that different polynomials of the same length have dramatically different error detection properties. For example, Wolf found a 32-bit polynomial that outperforms the standard CCITT polynomial by an order of magnitude for some burst lengths, and two 32-bit polynomials can differ by four orders of magnitude in detecting 33-bit bursts.

CRC32C (also called CRC32/4) uses the polynomial 11EDC6F41 (in bit-vector notation). It has a design distance of 6 up to block lengths of 5275 bits and distance 4 up to 2^31-1 bits, making it superior to the IEEE-802 CRC (polynomial 104C11DB7) which has only distance 4 at most.
sections.plainLanguage: CRCs use mathematical formulas to detect errors. Some formulas are much better than others at catching damage. Scientists have found special formulas that are nearly perfect.

sections.title: Burst Error Detection
sections.content:
Burst errors (consecutive corrupted bits) are detected differently than scattered errors. The RFC analyzes the probability of undetected burst errors for CRC32C using published research. Wolf's work shows that for a burst of length 33, the maximum probability of undetected error is approximately 4 × 10^-10.

The RFC derives probabilities for longer bursts by using the Rayleigh density function to model burst length distribution (with most bursts around 3 bits). For an 8 kilobyte block at a burst error rate of 10^-10, the analysis shows that the probability of an undetected burst error is approximately 10^-40 per block—well within the 10^-45 target.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if multiple bits in a row get corrupted—which is the most common kind of error—CRC32C will catch it almost all the time.

sections.title: Single Bit and Checksum Errors
sections.content:
For independent single bit errors (not in bursts), the RFC compares CRC against alternative checksums like Fletcher and Adler checksums. Research by Castagnoli shows that for 8 kilobyte blocks at a bit error rate of 10^-11, CRC32C and IEEE-802 both achieve undetected error probabilities of 10^-20. This is approximately 12,000 times better than Fletcher checksums and 22,000 times better than Adler checksums.

The RFC demonstrates that checksums are vulnerable to undetected errors due to their weakness in detecting burst errors. A simple example: if three consecutive bytes have error values x, -2x, x (in checksum arithmetic), the error is undetected. This pattern alone has a probability of 2^-16 per 3-byte burst, which for an 8 kilobyte block results in undetected error probabilities around 10^-16—far worse than CRC's 10^-40 target.
sections.plainLanguage: CRC is about 12,000 times better than simple checksums at catching random bit flips. Checksums miss too many errors to be trusted for important data.

sections.title: Hardware Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC compares the hardware complexity of implementing various CRC polynomials. Using tools to generate Verilog code for different polynomials and data widths, the RFC shows that CCITT-CRC32 requires significantly fewer logic gates than CRC32C. For a 32-bit datapath, CCITT-CRC32 requires only 40% of the gates needed for CRC32C. However, in a typical 1-million-cell chip, the CRC circuit represents less than 1% of the total size.

The RFC also demonstrates two implementation approaches: serial (processing one bit at a time) and parallel (processing 32 or more bits per clock cycle). Parallel implementations are much faster and are the standard approach in software implementations using lookup tables. The document includes Verilog code examples for both serial and parallel CRC32C implementations to help hardware designers.
sections.plainLanguage: CRC32C is slightly more expensive to build in hardware than some alternatives, but the cost is tiny compared to the rest of the chip.
